newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: OSCE calls on Milosevic to grant protesters' demands.
newsitem.headline: OSCE calls on Milosevic to grant protesters' demands.

text.p: Europe's biggest security body increased the pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Thursday, urging him to go beyond piecemeal concessions and give total recognition to opposition local election victories.

The OSCE admonished Belgrade after Milosevic convened federal Yugoslavia's security council to address the Serbian political crisis, which showed no sign of subsiding after the opposition resumed protest rallies despite the concessions.

Up to half a million people have demonstrated daily for almost nine weeks in a bid to reinstate opposition victories in Serbia-wide local elections nullified by the ruling Socialists (SPS), who claimed unspecified "irregularities".

Cornered by an OSCE inquiry that confirmed the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition had fairly won the vote in 14 of 18 major towns, electoral commissions on Tuesday admitted the ruling leftist coalition had lost Belgrade and Nis.
But the SPS-led commissions stressed the results were preliminary and the government had until Saturday to appeal.
That left ample room for legalistic delays and outright sabotage by hardline Socialists in the absence of clear direction from Milosevic, who has remained silent.
Suspicious opposition supporters vowed to continue protests after a senior Socialist hardliner said an appeal was planned.

"Step-by-step concessions to the opposition on what ought to be a merely mechanical issue -- translating the results into seats -- is simply not the way to handle this situation," OSCE chairman-in-office Niels Helveg Petersen said.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, commissioned an inquiry last month by former Spanish premier Felipe Gonzalez. He concluded that the annulment was fraudulent and called for the November 17 vote results to be respected.

"The situation in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (F.R.Y.) is a fast evolving one. On one point it has, however, not been fast enough," Petersen, the Danish foreign minister, told a session of the OSCE's permanent council in Vienna.
"The Permanent Council at its first session this year endorsed (Gonzalez's) conclusion," he added.
The OSCE remained open to dialogue with Milosevic's government to help solve the "profound political crisis".
"Our door is wide open. But the F.R.Y. does not seem to want to walk through it," Petersen said.
The reclusive Milosevic has cut back meetings with Western diplomats during the imbroglio and is thought to have been non-committal with the few visitors he has agreed to see.
Petersen said that without democratic reform in Serbia, ruled by authoritarian leftists, formerly communists, since World War Two, there was no chance to resolve the situation.
"The OSCE message to the Socialists is simply: 'Don't think you can get away with tossing bits and pieces of bones to the opposition'," a senior diplomat in Belgrade said.

"Serbia is being told to accept the Gonzalez report in full if it wants to get the international community off its back and back on its side so far as being re-admitted to international institutions after the end of U.N. sanctions."
Most of the sanctions, imposed in 1992 to punish Milosevic for instigating Serb separatist war in Bosnia, were lifted last year after he signed the Dayton peace agreement.
Diplomatic sources said Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic went to Madrid on Wednesday for meetings with Spanish officials but the result was not immediately known.
Federal Yugoslavia's Supreme Defence Council, grouping the presidents of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro but dominated by Milosevic, met on Wednesday evening to discuss the crisis.

A statement issued after the meeting and quoted by the official news agency Tanjug said the council "lent its support to the Republic of Serbia to resolve - within the institutions of its political system - the problems which have arisen in a number of municipalities over the local elections.
"This would make a significant contribution to strengthening the overall stability of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and enhancing its reputation in the world."

Diplomats said Milosevic may have convened the council to assess the loyalty of key officials including the Yugoslav army chief of staff and the Montenegrins, both of whom have indirectly criticised the Socialists' handling of the crisis.
